title: A Conversation at Jacob's Well
overview: Jesus crosses a deep religious and social divide to talk with a Samaritan woman, which leads many in her town to believe in him, and then he heals an official's son from a distance.

parts.label: Leaving Judea (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Jesus leaves the south because the Pharisees, a strict and influential religious group, had noticed his following was growing fast. On the way north he passes through Samaria and rests, tired, at noon by a well linked to the ancestor Jacob.

parts.label: The request for water (vv. 7-15)
parts.note: Jews and Samaritans were longtime rivals over ancestry and the right place to worship God, so a Jewish man asking a Samaritan woman for a drink was startling. Jesus speaks of "living water," a phrase for fresh flowing spring water, as a picture of a life from God that satisfies in a way no well can.

parts.label: Her story and true worship (vv. 16-26)
parts.note: Jesus shows he knows her past; the text never says why she had five husbands, and since men could end marriages more easily than women, many modern readers caution against assuming she was immoral. When she raises the old dispute over worshiping on nearby Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem, Jesus says the time has now come when worship depends not on a place but on God's Spirit and truth, then tells her plainly he is the Messiah, the promised deliverer.

parts.label: Food and a ripe harvest (vv. 27-38)
parts.note: The disciples are surprised to find their teacher talking publicly with a woman, while she leaves her water jar behind and goes back to tell the town. Jesus says doing God's work is what truly feeds him, and he compares the Samaritans now coming toward him to fields already ripe for harvest.

parts.label: Many Samaritans believe (vv. 39-42)
parts.note: Many Samaritans believe because of the woman's word, and many more believe after Jesus stays with them for two days. They call him "Savior of the world," meaning he belongs to more than one people.

parts.label: An official's son healed (vv. 43-54)
parts.note: Back in Galilee, a royal official, probably serving the local ruler Herod Antipas, begs Jesus to come heal his dying son, and Jesus simply tells him his son will live. The man trusts the word before seeing any proof, and the fever turns out to have broken at that very hour.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read the Samaritan woman at the center of this chapter: some see a sinner whose conscience Jesus gently exposes, while others see an outsider, possibly widowed or cast off, whom Jesus treats with dignity and who becomes one of the first to spread word about him.
think: Who in your own world would you find it hardest to sit down and talk with, and what makes that distance feel so wide?
